What steps are being taken by our government to suppress or prevent undesirable publications from entering Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. LAPOINTE (For the Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Department of National Revenue
Section 11 of the Canada Customs Tariff, 1907, provides that;-"The importation into Canada of any goods enumerated, described or referred to in schedule C to this act is prohibited; and any such goods imported shall thereby become forfeited to the crown and shall be destroyed or otherwise dealt with as the Minister of Customs directs; and any person importing any such prohibited goods, or causing or permitting them to be imported, shall for each offence incur a penalty not exceeding two hundred1 dollars."
Item 1201, schedule "C" of the Customs Tariff, 1907, classifies as prohibited goods:- "Books, printed paper, drawings, paintings, prints, photographs, or representations of any kind of a treasonable or seditious, or of an immoral or indecent character."
Collectors or other customs officers seize goods which are obviously immoral or indecent, and if their importation is general, as in the case of a publication, a circular is issued prohibiting its importation into Canada. Imported publications, concerning which doubt exists, are forwarded to the department by collectors, and other persons, and are carefully examined. If found to be of the character set forth in item 1201 of the tariff, they are prohibited.
Post Office Department Undesirable publications are being prohibited transmission in the mails under paragraph (d) subsection 1 of section 9 of the Post Office Act as amended in 1913.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the time has come for the establishment of a national system of banking.	[DOT]
He said: Mr. Speaker, in 1925 I moved a resolution looking in the direction of such action in these words:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is not in the interests of the country at large that the privilege of issuing currency and of controlling financial credit should be granted to private corporations.
In 1926 I moved a resolution similar in terms to that now under discussion. I recognize very [DOT] clearly that a fully developed system of national banking is not immediately practicable. In fact, the terms of my resolution have been criticized by some of my friends as suggesting that we would at once wipe out all private banks. That is by no means the thought behind the resolution. On the other hand, some have suggested that we already have a national banking system. But I do not think that it will1 seriously be contended that the present system is "national" in the sense of being nationally controlled. My resolution would look to a larger measure of control of the existing chartered banks, and more than that, towards more widespread public banking facilities. In my speech two years ago in support of the resolution I then moved I said that it seemed to me there were certain measures which might be adopted. First of all, currency should be issued by the government. Secondly, our postal savings banks should be developed and modernized and freed from red tape. men generally throughout the country asked themselves whether they were getting that opportunity for development which might be afforded if there were a wider distribution of financial control. My contention is that a few men not directly responsible to the people are able to manipulate the whole of the money and credit of the country in their own interests. Perhaps we in the west feel this more keenly than do the people in eastern Canada. We all know that the two great banking centres in Canada are Toronto and Montreal. All the institutions are centred there and we often feel that industrial concerns that have their headquarters in these two cities are apt to get credit facilities that are not accorded in the same measure to other institutions with headquarters in other parts of the country. In fact, I am not so sure that throughout Canada there is not a rising feeling that Canadian money ought not to flow so easily and freely to enterprises outside the Dominion. Why should Canadian money be sent to Cuba or Mexico or various republics in South America when apparently we require money for purposes of development in this country itself?
Some hon. gentlemen may remember a rather remarkable statement made during the election of 1925 by Sir Clifford Sifton. He said:
We are rapidly approaching that condition in which two or at most three banks will be doing the whole of the business of the Dominion and you will have the spectacle of about three men sitting on the whole of the funds of the people of Canada deposited in the banks and deciding to whom they will loan these funds.
And again:
If anything would justify an armed rebellion against the established condition of affairs I think such a consummation of our banking system is the one thing that would justify it.
Sedition.

Somebody suggests that this is sedition. Well, such an utterance might be seditious in the mouths of some of my comrades in the working class, but I suppose it is comparatively safe for Sir Clifford Sifton to make this statement.
I ask, in the next place, why should the banks be given the valuable franchise of issuing currency? Long ago certain people approached the great teacher of that day and asked him a question concerning taxation. He produced a penny and put this query to them:	Whose image and superscription is
this? I would produce two bank notes, first, a dollar bill, and would ask the same question: Whose is the image and superscription? And the answer?-King George's. But I
produce a ten dollar bill and when I ask the same question-whose image and superscription does this bear?-the answer is: the image and superscription of Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor and the image and superscription of Sir Vincent Meredith. In Canada, it would appear, the one dollar bill is good enough for the king, while with the fives and tens and everything higher, quite evidently, we admit the sovereignty of the money kings. There are some gentlemen in this house who sometimes upbraid us for what they regard as our lack of patriotism. Let me say to my patriotic friends to-day, "Help me to put the king's image and super scription on every bill in Canada."
I want now to pass on to a still more important consideration, namely, the control of credit. I take it that credit to-day is recognized as the life blood of trade; we cannot do business nowadays without credit. We all recognize how essential it is. And yet, as I pointed out a little while ago, credit is concentrated in the hands of comparatively few. More than that, I say that credit largely determines the purchasing power of the dollar. A few years ago a farmer said to me, "I am not going to put my money in the bank any longer; I am going to keep it in my jeans where it will be safe". I remarked, "You don't know the power of the banks. You may put your dollar into your pocket and fancy that it is safe, but when it comes out it may be worth only fifty cents". That is high class juggling, and in all seriousness it is the power which is possessed by private corporations to-day.
I wish to spend a few minutes on this economic aspect, which I know is not altogether easy; it is a technical question. It has been generally recognized that the amount of money in circulation is closely connected with the price level. Some practical bankers, absorbed in the routine of their business and thinking of currency only, are apt to take the position that changes in the price level lead to the expansion or contraction of the volume of money in circulation. Other bankers of note and most economists lay stress on the fact that the amount of money largely determines the price level. I am not going into that rather technical question, but I would quote such a leading economist as Professor Taussig, who says:
Double the quantity of money, and, other things being equal, prices will be twice as high as before and the value of money one-half. Halve the quantity of money, and other things being equal, prices will be one-half of what they w e r e before and the value of money double.

That is, prices as measured in terms of money.

Yes, as we always do measure prices. When there was only gold in existence, the expanding trade of the world had to be taken care of by the discovery of new deposits of gold until the invention of bank notes came about. That helped immensely; in fact, without bank notes I do not see how the enlarged trade of the world possibly could have been taken care of. There was still the old fashioned theory that the bank notes represented gold, but during the war we learned that gold was not of any very great consequence after all, but that the quantity of bank notes might alter the cost of living. We all know what happened in Germany and Russia, and later on in France; the printing presses were set to work, and the faster the money was printed the less that money was worth, and conversely the higher the cost of living rose. So we learned that it was not merely the quantity of gold which determined the cost of living but the quantity of bank notes in circulation as well.
That is generally accepted now, but I would submit that there is a third kind of money.
I know the bankers do not like to admit that it is money, but we have very good authority for calling it such. I refer to the chequeing system, because it is by the chequeing system to-day that we do some 96 per cent of the business of Canada. Cheques function as money, and I submit that the amount of credit issued affects the price level, or in other words the purchasing power. If you put so much more gold into circulation you send prices up; if you put so many more bank notes into circulation you raise the price level, and if you extend the credit of the country without extending the volume of business you also raise the price level. This is the most important matter in this connection, yet over this extension or contraction of credit the government has absolutely no control. The only way you can increase the quantity of gold is to discover new gold fields or to improve the processes of mining; the control of bank notes comes either directly or indirectly under the government, but the extension or the contraction of credit is a matter entirely under the authority of the banks themselves.

In the conditions of that situation I was reluctant to acquiesce, and I began to fight against it by financial self-assertion from the first	 I was tenaciously opposed by the governor and deputy governor of the bank, who had seats in parliament, and I had the eity for an antagonist on almost every occasion.

It has often been a surprise to me to hear that so much foreign capital is sought to develop Canadian industry, and I have wondered why it is necessary to go outside for this help. We know perfectly well that industry is carried on by a system of loans, those loans being made possible by the collateral that is placed at the disposal of the financial institution making the loans; that only on the basis of the collateral are loans made, and that those loans create current deposits that can be drawn on by the borrowers. Now, if this Canadian collateral is good enough for financial houses in the United States, Great Britain or elsewhere, why is it not good enough for our financial houses? Is it that the}1' are too conservative in character? If so, we cannot blame the other institutions making a harvest on the profit of these loans. But I should like to see Canadian financiers taking a little more interest in Canadian development, because the collateral is just as good a security to them as to outsiders.
I would favour some sort of a institution in the shape of a federal bank of re-discount for various reasons. Believing it would be a great boon to the country in every way, I would recommend the formation of such a bank for the following reasons:
1.	It could perform the duties now carried out by the treasury board by discounting securities of present or future banks.

2.	It could take over certain duties now carried out by the Canadian Bankers' Association witih regard to notes.
3.	It could serve the purpose of the central gold reserve.
4.	The note circulation redemption fund could be handled by it.
5.	Through it could be done all government business.
6.	It could and should issue all notes.

It is important that he make that point clear, because his speech does not tally with that of the mover of the resolution. In my opinion it should be entirely government business; it is more on the basis of the Australian bank. In conclusion, I cannot do better than quote from a speech delivered by the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna to the shareholders of the Midland bank in 1826 when advocating reform of the Bank of England. At the close of his address he said:
The subject is too large to permit of my entering into detail on an occasion like this, but I am convinced that it merits the most disinterested and painstaking investigation. An exhaustive inquiry into the principles on which a central bank should be founded and should conduct its operations would be of immense service to the public. The present system may have suited conditions in 1844, when deposit banking was in its infancy. It might conceivably suit conditions to-day, but if so only as the result of accident. It has survived for eighty years by virtue of its own .suspension in times of crisis, the phenomenal supersession of the use of currency by that of cheques, and fortuitous discoveries of gold. The vital need for the future is to ensure that the maintenance of prosperity with a growing population and ever-improving standard of living, both requiring an expansion in the volume of trade, shall not be hampered by false restrictions on the quantity of the money.

I wish
to add my voice to what has been said in support of the motion, not because I can better present the case than it has already been submitted by the mover of the resolu-

National Banking-Mr. Evans
tion (Mr. Woodsworth), and my hon. friend (Mr. Spencer). This is a business that touches the life of all industry and for that reason I wish briefly to cite some of my own experiences to show the absolute power which is placed in the hands of bankers over credit and industry to-day. In the banking system we have another of those public utilities in private hands controlled and operated for private profit, rather than for service to the people. There are in this nation many things which the people use, such as railways, the telegraph, the telephone, transportation and express services, and so forth, which Can rightly be called public utilities. And a public utility should never be in private hands to make profit for private companies; it should always be publicly owned and operated at cost. It is only on that basis that the industry of any country can assume the proportions it should when credit is free to all who may be able to use it.
Of all public utilities, I believe the banking business in private hands has become now about the most unbearable, not because it does not give service-service it does give- but from the fact that the more service it gives the more intolerable it is felt to be. It profits on the adversity of the people who have to avail themselves of it, and this is so because of the great power that comes from the concentration of wealth and industry. It is likely that the reports of the last annual meetings-I have not been able to peruse them all myself-will show that our banking system this year will make many millions of dollars of profit out of the earnings of the people, so that industry in the coming year will be so much more dependent on those who now control credit. No small business man to-day can get any moderate amount of money from the banks under about 9 per cent-and when I say 9 per cent I know exactly what I am speaking of because I am speaking from experience. It is thus that men in a small way are closed out, with the result that industry is still further concentrated in the hands of the few. Not only do these directors of industry concentrate control of business by granting or withholding credit as they see fit, but they are ever on the lookout for any renegade banking business which is not part and parcel of the banking association. I can remember when more than forty chartered banks existed in this country, when the population was indeed not over two-thirds of what it is to-day. It is quite evident that these big institutions entirely control the credit and industrial activities of the nation. When such concerns
as, for instance, the Merchants' Bank and the Bank of Hamilton of past days found it hard sailing they were taken in tow by the stronger banks. But this was not so in the cases of the Home Bank and the Farmers' Bank. In connection with the Bank of Hamilton and some others, there was no problem of compensating the depositors, as in the case of the Farmers' Bank and also the Home Bank. This latter institution was under attack from the banking combine from the time of its first appearance, and I can well remember when the Grain Grower^ Grain Company did their banking business with this bank. I can remember later on when an attempt was made to wreck both the Home Bank and the Grain Growers' Grain Company, and these two institutions were only saved at that time by the timely intervention of the Scottish Co-operative Wholesale Company, which then had representatives in this country. The Home Bank was always looked upon as a renegade and usurper by those who held the legal right, given by this parliament, to prevent the workers and farmers from using their credit, and to fleece them of their earnings. Indeed, sir, to further draw on my experience, I can clearly remember loading a car of wheat on the siding at Saskatoon, after having to wait several days and travel around a good deal before I got the car. When that car was filled I took my bill of lading to the chartered banks in that city, of which there were five at that time, and asked for an advance of $300 on that car of wheat, which was worth from $850 to $900 at least. I was refused by each of the five banks. Having returned to the bank with which I used to conduct my business, the then Bank of Hamilton, I pleaded with the manager to let me have $300 in order to meet an instalment due on a mortgage on my farm. He said, "The only thing wrong with that bill of lading is that it has the wrong name on it." My car was billed to the Grain Growers' Grain Company, which afterwards became the United Grain Growers. The manager said, "You take that back and change the name and I will give you all the money you want." I did not do so; I ran [DOT] the risk, and managed to meet my obligation only three days late.
These experiences only go to show the complete control exercised by these men over eveiy industry and activity of this nation; because the Grain Growers' Grain Company was doing business with the Home Bank, both these institutions were to be put out of business, and I was up against it. I say that banking is the business of the

National Banking

Mr. Evans
people, and it should be done by the government to a greater extent than is now the case. I think we should begin with a central government bank, to have the sole right of note issue and to provide for full discount privileges, so that the requirements of all producers could be adequately met at rates of interest which would only cover the cost. I believe this to be necessary at this time, and I want to tell this house that production on the farms of Canada is hampered to-day because of the lack of this measure. I believe we have come to the time when industry and credit and the sole control of the activities of the nation should not be left in the hands of a few private persons for their own personal benefit. It is a wrong *principle.
I believe further that a system of education should be inaugurated in order to make the people of Canada alive to this bondage which is so hampering the activities of our country. Surely it is not too much to expect that those occupying chairs of economy in our educational institutions from one end of the Dominion to the other should come forward with something worth while in language everyone can understand, but because the control of industry and credit has fallen into the hands of a few people who form such a complete ring, even the mouths of our chief educationalists have been closed for years past, and nothing is forthcoming even from our great professors of economy looking to the emancipation of the working classes and the small producers. We cannot go on forever in this way, with every moneyed interest and industrial concern linked up with the politician. For that reason I say the politician is the keystone in the arch, which is absolutely wrong in this advanced age, with an intelligent people such as we have in Canada to-day.
There are several reasons for this reform, and the first is to prevent the autocratic control of credit, which means the autocratic control of industry, and the control of the rates of interest and the power of inflation and deflation, from which we have suffered so much since the war. We should also pie-vent the investment of the earnings of the workers abroad, to the detriment of the development of our own national resources, which has a good deal to do with the unemployment existing at present. Surely it is evident to everyone that these things are needed, because it seems quite possible that the factors which made the lot of thousands of farmers so hard since the war may come about again; it is not such a remote possibility. If I read the newspapers aright I

can see a tendency even to-day to bring about war between the two greatest nations of the world, who can pay the most for their ammunition should there be another great struggle. For these reasons and also to bring the matter just as it is before the people of this country I propose to support the resolution.

Under the Australian

Mr. BOTHW'ELL:	I have no objection

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say that personally I have no objection to the resolution going before the banking and commerce committee. But I do take exactly the same exception to its wording as does my hon. friend from Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell), and I hope that if it is referred to the banking and commerce committee for further inquiry and study my hon. friend who hasl presented it will confer with the hon. member for Swift Current and so modify his resolution that the house will not be understood to declare that Canada has not a national system of banking. Because, Mr. Speaker, I submit that when you compare the banking system and the bank failures of Canada in recent years with the bank system and bank failures of any other country in the same period, there can be no doubt that Canada has much reason to be proud of her system.
May I say at once that I have no pretensions to expert knowledge of banking. My experience with bankers has largely been that of a borrower, and the greatest kindness they have ever done me was when sometimes they refused to loan me money, for money borrowed must be paid back. And I submit to my hon. friend that when they ask the Dominion to go directly into the banking business-and I believe they are men of good judgment-it would seem that they have not carefully reviewed the record of the experience of the government in loaning money out in that particular part of the country which they represent.
National Banking-Mr. Robb

Now, there is one feature, sir, that I desire to put on record. In the first place, my hon. friend in moving his resolution took some exception to the business that Canadian banks have been doing outside Canada, and he emphasized the point by asking:	Why
should we send Canadian money into other countries when it is needed at home for home development? Well, had my hon. friend carefully reviewed the published statements that are sent to the Department of Finance every month, he would have learned that our Canadian banks in doing business in other countries in competition with the banks of other nations are bringing more money into this country than they are sending out. Let me give the house the statement to December 31 last. My hon. friend can check up the records for each month and get the average. According to the published figures the aggregate commercial loans of Canadian banks elsewhere than in Canada were $264,708,072, and the aggregate deposits $374,425,788; or $110,000,000 more was received in deposits than paid out in loans in those countries. That money was available whenever Canada needed it. My hon. friend will observe that I am speaking of commercial loans. It is true that our banks had other deposits and other liquid loans outside of Canada. But the reason Canadian banks make these liquid loans outside the Dominion, largely in New York and in London, is that there is no liquid investment for the money at home, and rather than have it lie idle it is sent to New York and to London, where, although it is earning small interest, it is available whenever Canada needs it for the requirements of her own commerce.
Before I take up more particularly what our own Canadian banks are doing, may I reply to the remarks of the chief whip of the United Farmers of Alberta group to the effect that while our system may be satisfactory for the east it is not satisfactory so far as the west is concerned. He thinks that wie should adopt another system and that the Dominion of Canada should go into the banking business, loaning money and making it available for all who want it in all parts of Canada and particularly of the west. If I do not do the hon. gentleman justice I want him to correct me.
That is entirely incorrect so far as my statements went. I advocated that the institution be used as a government bank only.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, we have had experience in loaning money. We know what it costs to IMr. Robb.]
loan money when governments go into the loaning business, for we have now on the books of the department over $2,000,000, loaned largely in 1915, and some of it loaned away back in 1880. This money was loaned on good seourity and to-day we cannot find the gentlemen who borrowed it, so that the department is considering the probability of the money ever being recovered. It is a question whether it will not be altogether lost.
Is the minister taking into account the tremendous inflation and deflation which occurred during those years and which operated detrimentally to the whole farming industry of western Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At the time that money was loaned in the west the security was considered ample. But that is not the only experience of loaning money that we have had in this country. We have loaned not only in western Canada but in all the provinces over $100,000,000 under the soldier settlement scheme. And what is the position when the banking business is brought into politics? Hon. gentlemen have come to parliament year after year and have asked the government to revalue the lands on which the money has been loaned, informing parliament that the soldiers were not able to meet their payments. Perhaps they were right; I am not saying that they were not. But the general result is that under the re-valuation legislation the country stands to lose about $16,000,000. That is our experience when Canada goes into the loaning business.
My hon. friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) made reference to the Australian system; he spoke of the Commonwealth Bank of the government of Australia and told what it was doing for that country. And my bon. friend who moved the resolution (Mr. Woods-worth) as well as the hon. member for Rose-town (Mr. Evans) complained that a small group of men, about sixty I think, comprising an interlocked directorate, were handling the big business of the country. Now what was the condition in connection with the Commonwealth Bank of Australia? That bank, until after the death of Sir Dennison Millar, was managed solely by Sir Dennison Millar, the man in control. He was a real czar, for even the treasurer of the commonwealth government had nothing to say. Sir Dennison Millar alone was president, general manager and board of directors. I have nothing to say against the Commonwealth Bank of Australia; it is a good bank.

Was he not responsible to the government?

National Banking-Mr. Robb

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps he was. He was an
excellent banker, a trained Scottish banker, brought up in one of the Scottish banks, and invited to assume absolute control of the Commonwealth Bank under the law. But what has been the record of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia as regards the loaning of money to farmers and business men in that confederation? The records show that most of the assets of the Commonwealth Bank consist of dominion and colonial loans. Investments in British colonial and commonwealth government securities comprise the great bulk of the business, while bills discounted, loans and advances to customers, and other sums due the bank constitute about per cent of its assets. As I say, investments in British colonial government securities, commonwealth government securities, fixed deposits, bills receivable in London, and so on, are the large proportion of the business of that bank. While therefore the Commonwealth Bank of Australia may be useful to the federal government in floating loans, it certainly is of very small special value to the commercial community of Australia and to the farmers. Hon. gentlemen say, "It is a splendid thing for the government of Australia to have gone into this business'. Well, I invite them to compare the financial position of Canada, when Canada goes into the markets of the world to borrow money, with the position of the government of Australia. I am not saying a word against Australia; I do not suggest to what extent she has been successful in making loans. But I do say that Canada has no lessons to learn from Australia in the matter of banking or so far as the credit of the country is concerned.
The important point to bear in mind is this: A bank has always to maintain national1 confidence, so that the savings of the people may be deposited with it and be used for commercial purposes, the money being distributed where it can earn money instead of, as under the old system, being tucked away in a stocking and remaining there, useless both to the person owning it and to the community. I say, therefore, that it is imperative in Canada that we should do everything possible to maintain confidence in our banking system.
Hon. gentlemen opposite tell us that the banks in Canada are being gradually absorbed into the larger institutions and that whereas years ago we had a considerable number of banks-I forget how many-we are reduced at the present time to eleven or twelve. That is true. But what is the reason? Why is it that the request comes to the government from time to time for the merging of banks? Why is it that that splendid little bank, with headquarters in western Canada-
The bank of Weyburn.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I am referring to an eastern bank that moved west. A few years ago, as Minister of Finance, I had to go there and urge upon one of the strong banking institutions of the country to take over that concern -I am referring to the Union Bank-simply because I feared that we should have in Canada, if this were not done, a condition worse than existed in the case of the Home Bank. Well, what led to that state of things? One reason was that the bank had probably advanced more money than it should have done to two particular ventures in western Canada. But there was another reason, just as there is another reason why banks to-day, in order to carry on, find it necessary to get their forces together. And what is that reason? It is this, that big customers themselves throughout the country desire to do business with a large bank.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite come from a part of the country where one of the largest mergers in Canada has taken place-the western wheat pool. I am in favour of this, but I would point out to these gentlemen that such a concern cannot do business with small banks; it requires an institution that is able to take care of its commitments. And the same thing that is going on in connection with the wheat pool is taking place in eastern Canada. I will be frank with the house and say that representations are made to us from time to time that, because of mergers and the desire of these mergers to avail themselves of banks that will properly take care of their business, the smaller banks are having hard sledding. These small banks say, " Some of our customers who used to do business with us are now looking for larger and stronger banks." These are questions that might be considered by the banking and commerce committee, but I submit to my hon. friends opposite-and I hope they will agree with me-that it is not a good thing to have it go out to the world that Canada has not now a national banking system. As a matter of fact, under the Finance Act, we have. This is not the first time the question has been proposed for submission to the banking committee. Hon. gentlemen will recall that it was submitted in 1923 and again in 1924. Experts were brought here from Washington and the matter was gone into. In the course of the debate leading up to the referring of a resolution to the 'banking committee the question was asked, Why should not Canada have a system similar to the federal reserve bank of the United States? A gentleman was brought here and appeared as
National Banking-Mr. Robb

a witness before the banking committee and he declared-his evidence may be referred to if hon. gentlemen wish-to consult it-that under the Finance Act we are in Canada providing economically all the facilities that are required for carrying on the business of the country, and that we are doing work equally as good as that performed by the federal reserve system in the United States. I mention this in support of the statement made by my hon. friend from Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) that Canada has now a national banking system. And when hon. gentlemen say that the banks are given the right to put out all the money issued, the records show that of the Dominion notes issued-apart from coins issued by the Dominion-on the 31st day of December, 1927 there were $220,835,000 of Dominion notes outstanding, while bank circulation at the same date amounted to $182,747,000. So there was then outstanding a greater amount of Dominion notes than bank notes.
Did not the greater part of that $220,000,000 comprise notes of large denominations used by the banks alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It meets the requirements 6f the country and the government receives a revenue for it. As regards advances under the Finance and Bank Acts, since 1914-15 we have received a total of $16,831,894 from the banks for circulation charges and $14,402,129 as special tax, a total of $31,334,023. It is true that, under the Finance Act the government has no authority to loan directly to the customer, and in the light of the experience which the government has had in connection with loans made for seed grain in the west, and under the Soldier Settlement Board throughout Canada, it is a good thing that we have not that authority. We have, however, authority to make loans to the banks on certain securities stipulated, and any bank requiring funds has no difficulty in getting all the money needed to carry on the general affairs of the country. The proof that the banks have no difficulty in getting money lies in the fact that conditions throughout the country are good. No one is complaining that there is any insufficiency of funds. We did hear, however, from the hon. member who presented the resolution a complaint to the effect that Canadian banks were doing business in other countries, sending Canadian money out of the country, while in the very next breath some other hon. gentleman complained that money was coming into Canada. This shows the difficulty of trying to satisfy everyone. You will see large headlines in the press asking the question, "Why allow

foreign capital to come into this country?" and at the same time somebody gets up in this house and declares that we should not allow our capital to go out. Now there is a happy medium, and while I repeat I have no objection to the resolution being studied by the banking and commerce committee, I must say I have a decided objection to advertising to the world at large that Canada has not a national banking system.

Does the minister not take
into account the fact that the great debt which the farmers of the west owe the government for seed and feed during the season of 1915 particularly is due not to any banking system but to the -fact that the price of wheat in 1917 was set at 50 per cent of its value? May I remind him that when the group which I charge with having the power of inflation and deflation decided upon deflation, wheat was the first thing that dropped, with the result that we had 2,000 farmers fewer between 1925 and 1926.

In rising to speak very briefly to the motion before the house I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. FEBRUARY 13, 1928
National Banking-Mr. Irvine
Woodsworth) upon his very admirable presentation of the theme, one which it is not easy to present to parliament in the short time in which he had to dispose of it. I wish also to say that I agree with the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) in the exception he took to the wording of the resolution. Next I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) for the very reasonable attitude which he adopted towards the proposal. I think he indicated that with certain modifications he would not oppose this resolution going to the committee. I think, Sir, that that is a very reasonable attitude. No one will deny that the subject in itself is one which covers a very wide field indeed, one which by its very nature is extremely technical, and that it would be very difficult for the house to discuss a subject of this kind and arrive at any conclusion that would be of service in the future. So that the committee is the only hope in a subject of this kind. This does not, of course, presuppose that the committee will find very much the matter, but it will afford us an opportunity of discussing the subject and investigating it thoroughly.
Now I desire before moving the amendment -which I hope will meet with the approval of the minister, for I have tried to draft it to meet the objections which he offered-to refer very briefly to some of the suggestions that the Minister of Finance made; because I do think that some of his remarks go perhaps a little beyond what he intended. Indeed, I doubt whether he would be willing to admit some of the implications of his remarks. The minister objected to the idea going forth that Canada did not have a national banking system. Now it may be that our banking system is a national system that may be what is the matter with our banking system, but I have never at any time thought that the mere nationalization of anything would cure it. I am not sure that the nationalization of our banking system, even if it were a fact or if we contemplated it, would be sufficient to meet the requirements of Canada to-day, having regard to her condition generally from an economic and an industrial point of view. I do not think that the question is so much who is carrying on the banking; the question is rather what is being done. I do not make a plea now for the nationalization of the system. I make a plea for service from the system, I want to see that system functioning in its proper relationship to the economic demands of the nation. I do not care whether that is done by a private bank or by a national bank. I do not even care if our bankers make some profit out of the transaction. The great trouble does not lie in the profits they make;
it lies in their control of a necessity of our economic life, and a control which is not always an intelligent one. During our investigations of recent years the bankers who appear before the standing committee frankly admitted to us that they did not understand the economic significance of finance. They understand, of course, the technique of banking; they are masters of finance in that respect, but they have, by their own confession, admitted that they do not understand the economic significance of finance. So that the greatest difficulty comes when they retard credit at times when credit ought to be released, and they release credit at the very moment when it ought to be retarded because they have not studied the economic side of the question. There, in my opinion, is where the big difficulty lies: not in the management of our banks, be it private or public, but rather in the fact that they are not being allowed to function in their proper relationship to the industrial demands of the country. On the other hand I do not think the minister really means to say that we have a national system at the present time. We certainly have not a national system in the ordinary sense of the term "national". Our system is national in a territorial sense, because our banks have branches scattered all over the Dominion, and our system may be regarded as a national system in so far as our banks have control over the economic life of the state; there is no doubt about that. We also have a national system in so far as the banks enjoy a privilege conferred upon them by parliament, and we may have a national system from some other points of view. But to say that we have a national banking system in the same sense that we have a national railway system-I do not think for one moment the minister really means that.
There is one other point which the minister mentioned upon which I wish to touch. He compared the credit of Canada with that of Australia when the two countries attempted to sell their bonds abroad. I am not in a position to know what are the respective positions of the two countries in that regard. I could however very easily see Why the credit of Australia might be impaired by financiers abroad if it be true that Australia has taken a step towards breaking the monopoly of finance in that country. That in itself might be a very good reason. However, I have not the figures, and therefore I must accept what the minister says in that regard without comment-
The point I want to emphasize more particularly is in regard to What the minister said with respect to the soldiers' civil reestablishment scheme. He characterized that
m
National Banking-Mr. Irvine

as a loan on the part of the Dominion of Canada along banking lines. Of course the minister knows very well that that is not the character of that transaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend speaks of
soldiers' civil re-establishment. W'hat I was speaking of was the soldier settlement board.

I accept the correction of
the hon. minister. The loan even in that regard was not a banking loan of the type we usually consider banking business. That loan, if the minister wishes to call it so-I do not accept for a moment that it is so, but for the sake of argument assuming that it is a loan, I want to point out to the minister just why it met with sutfh disastrous results as he has indicated, and I do not think the minister will attempt to say that my analysis is wrong because the facts are too patent to admit of contradiction. Is it or is it not a fact that the money in that loan to the soldier settlement board was expended largely upon lands which were purchased at the time when we were at the peak of inflation, and that the settlers were expected to repay that loan when the prices they received for the commodities which they produced had dropped to the very bottom in a period of deflation? To expect them to repay the loan undeT such conditions was on the very face of it ridiculous. But I want to inquire 'how it happened that we had inflation, and how it happened that we had deflation.
What were the peculiar circumstances which made the one hundred cent dollar of Canada in one year worth only forty-five cents the next year? To make a long story short, that occurred because we did not have intelligent financial control in Canada. That is why it happened. And who had the control, sir? The bankers' association had control, and those were the fruits of their work. The minister indicates that we have in the treasury board an institution which functions in exactly the same capacity as a federal reserve system would function. If that is so does the minister accept responsibility for the difference between inflation and deflation which occurred in the transaction to which he referred as a failure in national banking? If I recall aright, both the present Minister of Finance and the preceding Minister of Finance refused to accept any responsibility in that regard. I think I am also right in saying that the bankers who were examined before the parliamentary committee in the investigation which took place on the credit question also refused to accept any responsibility for that situation. Since neither the treasury board nor the

bankers' association will accept responsibility for what takes place through the instrument which they are both supposed to be handling, I can only come to the conclusion that there is nobody handling it, that it is handling itself, that it is simply running wild, that there is no control.
Some hon. member said that we were wanting easier money, more credit let loose. At the moment I am not so sure but that we want less credit let loose. There is just as much harm in too much credit as in too little credit. Let there be no mistake about what we want in this regard. We want control. We do not want this thing to run wild either in one direction or in the other.

Can the hon. member
tell us how those countries got along with respect to inflation and deflation which had the type of state banking which he is discussing?

I am not advocating a
national banking system. I thought I made that clear at the outset of my remarks, when I said as clearly as I could that perhaps what was the matter with the system we have in Canada now was that it is a national system; for the minister has said that it is. I do not for one moment think that if you nationalize the system we have now it would be any more efficient. What is wrong is that nothing is being done so far as control is concerned. Who is controlling this matter, and what is being done? Nothing whatever so far as control is concerned; and my authority for making that statement is the refusal of the Minister of Finance during the period of depression to accept responsibility for that depression, and the refusal of the representatives of the bankers' association before the parliamentary committee to accept any responsibility at all for that situation. I repeat that if both the treasury board and the bankers' association refuse to accept responsibility either for inflation or deflation, then I must conclude, as every other person must who thinks about the matter, that there is not any agency controlling the financial system of Canada, and I say it is control that we want. We are not asking that any institution shall let loose too much credit, or too little credit. We believe this is a mathematical problem, that the data necessary to arrive at a correct conclusion is not beyond the possibility of human intelligence to get, and that if it is within the grasp of human intelligence, that then the dread conditions which have followed both inflation and deflation ought to be stopped, and this parliament ought to accept the responsibility for stopping it.

National Banking-Mr. Cahill
This subject, as I have said, covers a very wide field. A very wide field has already been covered by previous speakers, and to make any specific pronouncement would require a very great deal of technique which I do not intend to ask the house1 to listen to at this time. I will have something further to say on this question when it arrives at the proper place for that kind of consideration, and that is in the committee. I shall not weary the house with any further remarks, but in the hope that the amendment I am about to propose will meet the objection raised by the Minister of Finance when he spoke to the resolution, I move:
That the resolution he amended by striking out all the words after the word "come" in the second line, and inserting therefor the following:
"For the consideration of the improvement of our banking system, and that the banking and commerce committee be instructed to study possible improvements and report thereon."

I crave your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, and the indulgence of the house for a moment while I extend to my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) my congratulations on his elevation to the honourable position of leader of the Conservative party. I trust he may live long to enjoy that distinction, and that he may long remain a leader of his majesty's loyal opposition.
I am glad that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has agreed to send to committee the resolution moved by the bon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). That the present banking system of Canada is inadequate to the needs of Canada is becoming apparent to a great many people throughout the country. I think the leader of the opposition will also agree with the resolution, at least to some extent. The other day he dwelt on the fact that we were losing many people from Canada. He lamented the emigration which has been taking place for some years, and I think if he will study this question of Canadian banking he will find the cause, in a great measure, of the emigration. The present system of banking, centralized as it is, will not permit of the development of Canadian resources by the Canadian people. Those who have given any study to governments or the organization of society have always attempted to get as far away as possible from centralized authority and centralized control; yet we permit that system in Canada in our banking.
We are told that ours is a wonderful banking svstem, that it is the best in the world. I think possibly, Mr. Speaker, that is because we know no other banking system, because
we were brought up with it. We are preached to from time to time and told that ours is a wonderful system, and as we have had no experience with any other we are naturally inclined to believe ours must be a good one. But any system of banking that will centralize the finances of the country in one or two cities cannot ,possibly be a good one for a country as extensive as ours is in point of area. It is just as necessary to have a financial structure in the country as it is to have engineers. My hon. friend who has moved the resolution and myself might build a railway from here to Winnipeg without an engineer. It would be a mighty poor railway,
I admit, but it would be possible to do it. Now, we are attempting to do the same thing in our finances-that is, to build a financial structure in Canada without trained financiers. You will say we have trained financiers and excellent bankers. I agree that we have some, but they are altogether too limited in number. Outside of the two great cities of Toronto and Montreal, you have in Canada practically no trained bankers. You have scarcely a man in a bank in Canada who is competent to give financial advice to his clients, or to the young people growing up in the country, who need the assistance, the aid and the advice of trained bankers. Under our system the banks employ boys, some from the high schools, others from the country store, and some who have not had even that training. In a few years they are themselves managers of branches of the bank, where their only function is to collect money from depositors in the district in which they are located and forward it either to Montreal or to Toronto.
I do not agree with much that was said by my hon. friend opposite about the banks not wanting to lend money. Every bank in the world is just as anxious to lend money as any man who is entitled to credit is to get that credit. Money is absolutely useless to a bank unless the bank can lend it. The bank cannot afford to pay three per cent on deposits and not lend that money; they must do it in order to make a profit; so that I have no quarrel with the banks so far as lending money is concerned. The quarrel I have with the present system is that the money is accumulated only in two large centres, and there are no facilities for lending money except in those two centres. As a result of that condition the banks, not having, as I say, the facilities to make loans other than in these cities, were forced to make improvident loans and suffer great losses, which brought down the number of banks from about thirty to something like ten or twelve. If you study the system you
National Banking-Mr. Cahill

will readily understand that a bank with four or five hundred branches could not possibly delegate to four or five hundred people the power of the central bank or the power of making loans. Necessarily they must consult with the head office. There must be some head to the institution, and the head is located only in two centres for all [DOT] of our banks. It is not so much the bankers that are at fault; it is the banking system and the system of establishing branches which will not permit of the development of the natural resources throughout the country.
The Minister of Finance pointed out that we do not have the failures that they have in other countries-I presume he had in mind the failures in the United States. Our banking system has very often been compared to that of the United States, where they have a system of small and large banks throughout the country. True, they have had many trifling failures, but these would not compare with the failures of our banks in any instance that I know of. They have had numerous failures throughout the agricultural districts of the United States in the past few years, but they were only small failures and dealt only with the money of the people in the community in which the bank was situated.
e are also told that this is an elastic system which admits of making large loans to the large mergers. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is something more required in Canada than banking facilities to take care of the large mergers. We want something that will take care of the young Canadian who is growing to manhood and attempting to develop industry in Canada, but who never has an opportunity of talking to a real banker during his younger days, and until he has reached the stage where he can go to Toronto or Montreal and consult with the real bankers of the Dominion there, nnd only there, he can never hope to establish a credit for himself. We all know that credit is the one essential to success in business, that no man can possibly succeed to any extent in business until by good management and integrity of conduct he has developed the confidence of his associates in his ability and straightforwardness. I repeat, he never reaches that stage because he has no banker to consult with. If he wants to finance an enterprise in Canada he must do one of two things, go either to Toronto or to Montreal where the head offices of our chartered banks are located'; otherwise he has no chance of talking to the financial people in this country.
The banking system of the United States- a system that is condemned in some quarters- has succeeded, Mr. Speaker, in developing 
every resource in every local community an the union. You cannot go from the Canadian boundary to Mexico or from Maine to California and find any resource capable of being profitably developed without being able immediately to get the necessary money right at hand. In Canada it is impossible to do this, and I fear that as a result our banking system has got us to the position where we are very little better off to-day than the people of Mexico. Twenty-five or thirty years ago they were quite willing to transact business with the Americans. They were willing to sell them their natural resources. It was all done legitimately and above board. But the Mexicans found later that they had sacrificed their resources and lost their control to outside people. Well, Mr. Speaker, we are coming to the same position. I read with interest a pamphlet issued periodically by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It contains a lot of valuable information and is well worth perusal by every hon. member. One number points out that in 1913 Canada owned only 30 per cent of her national debt, that is, the bonds were in Canadian hands; but in 1923 or 1924 we owned practically 70 per cent-'representing, I presume, in the neighbourhood of seven or eight hundred million dollars. The writer also points out that in recent years three or four billion dollars of outside money has been invested in Canada.
Now, I want again to say a word to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance on this point. To my mind, it is not good business to sell to the Canadian people our low-priced government bonds, for it follows that the Canadian who is attempting to develop industry must go elsewhere and pay high prices for his money. It would be much better for the minister to float his bonds outside Canada, and thus leave our domestic funds for the development of our natural resources. We find that great sums of money are being spent here. I am glad to see it, it is a good thing to have the capital available, but it should be spent under Canadian management, if possible; and it would be possible had we had a system of banking that would have developed a number of financiers of this country. They would have been able to finance such enterprises through Canadian banks, and also through outside banks with the help of Canadian banks. How much better this would be for the Dominion than selling our natural resources to outsiders, who will take the dividend cheque out of the country and give us the labourers' cheque-the dinner pail. I regret to have to say so, but we are fast approaching the stage where we will have the opportunity of carrying the dinner

National Research-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
pail instead of cutting the dividend coupon, and I think our banks are more responsible for that undesirable condition that any other agency in Canada.
Except the government.

Perhaps so; perhaps the government should have amended the Bank Act long ago in such a way that it would have been useful to the Canadian people. I cannot convince myself, Mr. Speaker, and I doubt if I could convince you or any person else in this house, that the Canadian people are not just as bright, just as energetic and just as able as any other people that we know of in the world. Why should we put ourselves in the position of having to take second place in our own country to others who come in here? I do not believe they are any smarter than Canadians, but they have a system of finance in which they are trained, just as our people are trained in any other profession. We lack that training, we cannot have it under our present banking system, and until we change that system there will be no practical advance in Canada. I agree with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that we have made no real progress in the last twenty or thirty years. True, we have gained somewhat in population. But how? We have simply traded our Canadian-born for a foreign population. I do not blame the present government, I do not blame the past government, but I do say that the time has come to study the Whole question with a view to the good of Canada, let the suggestion come from where it may. If we do not, if we continue along present lines, there will soon be mighty few Canadians left in the country, for, as I have said, we have maintained our population so far by importing people whom we at least claim are not quite as good as our native-born.
This condition, Mr. Speaker, has gone on for years and years. It is only coming to a head now with the formation of gigantic mergers. It is only now we are beginning to realize that the Canadian has not developed his natural resources; it is only now we are beginning to realize that locally our natural resources have not been developed; it is only now we are coming to realize that our money is going to Toronto or Montreal, if not to New York; and if it is not too late to study the question, it is certainly not a moment too early. Therefore I hope, Sir, that the government will offer every facility for the study of this whole question, and will lend their assistance in devising ways and means of bringing about a better financial structure for Canada
through a better banking system, and so give to the Canadian his proper heritage instead of forcing him to leave his own country to seek a livelihood.
Is the house ready for the question?
Carried.

I declare the main motion, as amended, carried.
Motion (Mr- Woodsworth) as aimended agreed to.
NATIONAL RESEARCH INSTITUTE Mr. E. J. GARLAND (Bow River) moved:
That in the opinion of this house, the time is now come when the further development ot our country requires the establishment ot a national research institute, and that this should be undertaken by the Dominion government.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, my chief excuse, if
excuse be needed, for addressing the house on this subject to-night is the apathy of the public on the need for a national research institute. The whole trend of my discourse I hope will be in the direction of sympathetic cooperation with what I understand the go\ -eminent has in mind. At the outset let me congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) on the statement- which I understand is correct-that there is to be included this year a large item in the estimates for the establishment of such an institute. I am not sure that I altogether agree that the amount proposed to be provided will be enough, but it is going to be a very healthy start in the right direction. It took the war to shatter the complacency not only of Canada but of England in regard to the matter of research. Prior to that time both countries had drifted along without worrying very much about what research meant, what it might do for the country, or anything else. Many of us had grasped theoretically the idea that Germany's great industrial progress was the result of the application of research to industry. It was not, however, I say, until the war itself that England and subsequently Canada realized the value of research in the development of their own resources and in the organization of their own industries.	^
We established a national research council and to that council belongs a great deal of credit for having maintained public interest during the years that have elapsed. It is true they have had a tremendous task. Public interest started waning in 1918 and it continued waning until a series of articles appearing in the press in 1927 again brought this question before the public. The amount that
412 .	COMMONS
National Research-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
is to be expended on this kind of an institute must from the very outset be adequate. At the present time research work is to a limited extent being carried on within our departments of government; our universities are trying to do something along that line, and a few of our larger manufacturing concerns maintain laboratories. But the government services are necessarily largely curtailed and localised;1 the work of the universities is almost entirely local, and the work of both the government and universities prior to this time has been diffused because of the necessity of carrying on partly educational work as well as research work at the same time. There is in Canada practically not one gentleman who is carrying on research work who is devoting his entire time to it. The other day I picked up an article that was printed in the Canadian Forum and I find that view supported by this statement,
Scientists in the direct employ of industry In this country are still occupied more largely with regulatory duties than with research. In fine, it is true that with pitifully few exceptions, there are no scientists in Canada whose whole business is research. Almost all are able to devote to research only what dregs of time and energy are left over from other important and often multifarious duties.
Does the hon. gentleman mean that in the broadest sense or in regard only to industrial research?

I am
dealing with research in its broadest sense.
Then that statement is absolutely wrong.

It was not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to take part in this debate until a few moments ago, and I rise now principally for two reasons. First, I want to contradiot a statement made by the previous speaker (Mr. Garland) that there is not a single man in Canada engaged in pure science. Second, I want to congratulate the government, especially the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), for the support they have given to this cause for a good many years. It is now nearly ten years since I first raised my voice in this parliament on behalf of scientific and industrial research, and as the years have gone by I have been more and and more impressed not only by the desirability but by the absolute necessity of Canada's indulging in some such form of assistance as is now proposed.
My criticism of the government on this particular occasion is two-fold. First, they are six or seven years too late; and secondly, the support which they are giving to scientific and industrial research is far too meagre. I



National Research-Mr. McGibbon
believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce is going to ask parliament to vote something like three-quarters of a million dollars for this purpose. If he had doubled, trebled, or quadrupled that amount, it would be more in keeping with the necessities of the case. The time has long since come when this country and every other country must use to the fullest possible extent all the advantages of science in order to keep pace with the other countries of the world. And in that connection, Mr. Speaker, I should not want it to go out to the world in the language of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) that the great country of Canada has not been able to produce a scientist; that the universities of this country have not made it possible for a single man in Canada to devote his or her whole time to science. I think, Sir, he must be sadly ignorant of the history of his own country, sadly ignorant of the history of his own province I recall to his mind certain names which have recently been placed on the honour roll of accomplishment in scientific research-such men as Professor Collip, of Alberta university, one of the principal assistants to Doctor Banting in perfecting the insulin discovery; Professor McCallum, of McGill university; Doctor Banting himself, of Toronto university and Professor Macleod, all of whom are devoting all their time and energy to scientific research. I should like to remind my hon. friend that Professor McCallum has made discoveries which have been recognized the world over. He has been offered the presidency of five universities and he is now devoting all his time to fundamental science at McGill.
Indeed, I do not have to go further than the city of Ottawa. May I direct attention to the discoveries of Doctor Watson and the work he is doing? Need I recall the fact that this government is completing a $70,000 building across the river, and also the remarkable result which Doctor Watson recently achieved in reducing an expenditure of $47,000 in connection with dourine compensation, first to $300 and later to $70? Might I call attention to the work done in the Department of Agriculture in developing the different grades of grain, a work which has meant millions of dollars of value to this country? I do this only to show that Canadians have not been behind in this field; that we have within our own borders men of intelligence, industry and ability in scientific and industrial research.
I should like to ask my hon. friend too, Sir, if he heard anything about the work of Canadians during the war. Are the scientists IMr. McGibbon.]
of Canada behind those of other countries? I should like to remind him of the great task placed on the shoulders of one Canadian during the war, a task equal if not superior to that performed by any other man during that period:	I refer to the closing of the strait
of Dover against submarines, a task which was given to a Canadian. Gathering about him a staff of Canadians, he and his assistants worked some twelve or fifteen months; the strait of Dover was closed in August, 1917, and not a submarine went through after that. What had been applied there could also be applied in the North sea, we are told, except for one portion which was too deep, and that could be looked after by other means.
I could refer also to the work of a Canadian in connection with the submarine telephone, a thing of inestimable value. I could recall the work in Toronto of Doctor Banting, who within the last few years discovered the secret of the treatment of diabetes. That was something scientists all over the world had been looking for, and it fell to the lot of a Canadian to make the discovery, one of inestimable value to mankind not only in the relief of suffering but in the prolonging of human life; and every year a man's life is prolonged through the application of that remedy means a natural source of revenue to the country.
I might go on, if time would permit, and point out to my hon. friend, to the house and to the country what the different pathologists, the great seekers of the unknown in all the universities of Canada, have been doing in the past, and to show to him that much as we admire immigrants, who come to our shores, we are not prepared to admit that the native born subject is inferior to any man on eatth.
I should like to congratulate the government upon the steps which they are taking in this matter. For ten year3 I have preached this doctrine in the house. I believe that for every dollar they expend they will receive ten-fold in return. I could give the house illustrations which I have put on Hansard in the past of the great returns which have been made on the money invested in scientific and industrial research. I could tell you, for example, of a discovery made by a firm in the American republic to the south where, by improving the grade of yeast, that single firm has saved $500,000 a year. I could refer you to the great Pasteur, and not only in the realm of medicine and surgery; I could tell you about his scientific work in France in connection with the silk worm, splenic fern and with wines

National Research-Mr. Malcolm
and other discoveries. The eminent Huxley stated that his three discoveries created enough wealth for the French republic to pay off the debt, for the Franco-Prussian war.
I could take you to the great industries of Canada and show you their magnitude. We have a fishing industry bringing in about $40,000,000 a year, and we are told by scientists that the waste of oil from the by-products is twenty-five per cent of the total value of the fish. I could point to the waste products of the saw mills and pulp mills and show you the possibilities of creating wealth from material that is now thrown away. I sat on a committee which gathered evidence some years ago, and we were told by scientists that an ordinary load of sawdust would produce ten gallons of ethyl alcohol, while one bushel of grain would only produce about three. Here is an opportunity for utilization of an absolute waste of the industries of this country to-day, material which is largely thrown into our streams and swamps. I could tell you of vast industries that were created during the war. For instance, Mr. Speaker, you will remember that early in the struggle our scientists told us that if Great Britain would only shut off the imports of cotton into Germany the war would be over in six months. When public opinion was brought to the point, and the blockade was put in force, what was the result? Germany put her scientists to work and from cellulose they developed a product to take the place of cotton-and the war went on. I could tell you that when Germany's imports of potash salts were restricted -and, of course, as everyone knows, these form the basis of fertilizers and other important things-the scientists of that country by an electrical process extracted nitrogen from the air and rendered Germany independent of the imported salts. I could tell you about the great artificial silk industry of this country which has been developed, how under pressure and through chemical processes cellulose is converted into artificial silk. Thus I might go on with one industry after another of the Dominion and Show how their development has been due to the application of science, and point out the possibilities of the future in this direction. This, sir, is the duty before the government. The waste in our forests today is awful to contemplate. In the heart of the country I come from you will see hemlock bark, which in past years was used for the tanning of leather, now allowed to rot, the cost of transporting it to the markets being prohibitive. Some years ago I pointed out to the research council the possibility of extracting the tanning material from the bark 56103-27*
by commercial processes. So far it has not been successfully done- But you can take countries like Germany, the United States and Great Britain and note how the application of science! to industrial research has brought about remarkable developments in various industries.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the government, because it is one of the few times that I can agree with its policy. Particularly do I congratulate my friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce that at last he has had the courage to imake a start on this path. I very heartily support him and the government in this policy. My only criticism tonight is that instead of asking for $750,000 they should bring down a requisition for at least $3,000,000. They will need the money in the next two or three years, and they know it. Then why not make a start, and make it with courage, and so give our industries the advantage of the latest scientific research? Let us put them on an equal footing with the industries of other countries. In a word, let us develop Canada for Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. JAMES MALCOLM (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay the house at any length tonight, but there are one or two observations that I should like to make now that this resolution presents the opportunity. Naturally it is very gratifying for a member of the government to have the support which has been given me by my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) and my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon). Indeed, I doubt if any other subject has met, or will meet, with as general approval from the house as the subject of the development of scientific and industrial research.
For many years outstanding men in this house have ' advocated increased expenditure on industrial research. Mr. Hume Cronyn raised his voice in this chamber on many occasions in season and out of season in his efforts to impress upon us the necessity of greater expenditure in this regard, and I believe the time has come when the public conscience has been awakened to an extent that will justify a forward movement in this field of endeavour.
May I compliment my friends from Bow River and Muskoka for having covered a great deal of the subject, which relieves me of the necessity of reviewing it to-night. I wish consequently to point out just two things. First, I appreciate the sincere criticism of my friend from Muskoka that we are not asking for a large enough vote. Let

National Research-Mr. Malcolm
me tell him that the $750,000 is being asked at the request of the national scientific and industrial research council. After going ovqr the whole matter with that body it was estimated that it would take about three million dollars during a period of five or ten years to construct the laboratories necessary at the capital to carry on this work. It was further felt however that in this year's program it was not possible to spend a greater sum for the first unit of the buildings than appears in the estimates. The council also asked for an increase from $170,000 to $300,000 for administrative purposes for the current year. That increase appears in our estimates. Thus in doing what we propose we are acting on the advice of the only body in Canada which is in a position to advise us. It is true we might have asked the house to vote a larger sum of money, but it could not be advantageously expended this year. The house must remember this fact, that the building up of the executive of the research council is a comparatively easy matter; we have many able public men in the Dominion who will be glad to join the board of the research council and give it the benefit of their advice. The building up of a trained staff to operate the laboratories, however, is a matter which will require time and very careful selection. At the moment there is not an unlimited number of men available with the necessary scientific knowledge to go into the pure science of the many subjects which we will undoubtedly have to take up, and tthe development of the laboratories will therefore of necessity be progressive. I hope in this connection that from year to year we shall be coming to parliament asking for ever-increasing sums of money as the work develops. I wish, too, to point out that there is a very considerable amount of scientific work being done by the various departments of government, and that this work will have gradually to be amalgamated with the work of the main laboratories. That amalgamation will take time, and the scientific men in the various government departments will gradually find themselves, as opportunities occur, working under one head. That is what we shall try to accomplish.
Now, as to any possible overlapping between federal and provincial endeavours in this field, may I say this? It is the opinion and advice of the national research council that Canada has within the various provinces many research problems which are entirely local. The council feels that from its vote it may be able to assist in research work on such local problems by contributions to a
[Mr Malcolm.]
university situated within the province. In that way provincial governments themselves, if they choose to vote further sums of money, will have such local research work under their own observation, so to speak. Without going into a discussion of the coal problem, wa know that we have very great fields of coal. We know that our Alberta coal is high in moisture content, and we know that one of the difficulties in coking our Nova Scotia coal is that it is high in sulphur content.
